terms.definition: An AI system that can take actions autonomously — reading files, calling APIs, running code, making decisions — not just generating text. Agents do work; chatbots give answers.
A structured way for software to talk to other software. When you send a prompt to Claude through code instead of a chat window, you're using an API.

The mechanism that lets AI focus on relevant parts of the input when generating output. It's why AI can connect "the cat sat on the mat" to a question about cats, even if the question comes 1,000 words later.
A prompting technique where you ask AI to reason step by step instead of jumping to the answer. It improves accuracy on complex tasks by forcing the model to show its work.
The text that an AI model generates in response to a prompt. You send a prompt; you get back a completion.
The maximum amount of text an AI can "see" at once — both your input and its output combined. Think of it as the model's working memory. Bigger windows let you feed more information.
An AI that generates images by starting with random noise and gradually refining it into a picture. Used by DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion.
A way to convert text (or images) into a list of numbers that captures meaning. Similar concepts get similar numbers, which is how AI can understand that "dog" and "puppy" are related.
Training an existing AI model on your own specific data to make it better at a particular task. Like teaching a general-purpose chef to specialize in Italian cuisine.
Rules and constraints you set to keep AI output safe, on-topic, and within boundaries. "Do NOT modify existing tests" is a guardrail. They prevent AI from going rogue on your codebase.
When AI generates information that sounds confident but is factually wrong. It doesn't "know" it's making things up — it's pattern-matching, not fact-checking. Always verify critical claims.
The process of running a trained AI model to generate output. When you send a prompt and get a response, that's inference. Training teaches the model; inference uses it.
The time between sending a prompt and receiving the first token of the response. Lower latency means faster responses. Affected by model size, server load, and network distance.
A massive AI model trained on enormous amounts of text data. Claude, GPT, and Gemini are all LLMs. "Large" refers to the billions of parameters (adjustable weights) that make them work.
An open protocol that lets AI models connect to external tools and data sources in a standardized way. Like USB for AI — one protocol, many tools. Created by Anthropic.
An AI that can process multiple types of input — text, images, audio, video — not just words. A multimodal model can look at a photo and describe what's in it.
The adjustable numbers inside a neural network that the model learns during training. More parameters generally means more capability, but also more compute cost. Claude has billions of them.
The input you give to an AI model — the question, instruction, or context that tells it what to do. Better prompts get better outputs. This is the skill most people underinvest in.
The art and science of crafting prompts that get the best results from AI. Includes techniques like role prompting, chain-of-thought, few-shot examples, and structured output.
A security attack where malicious instructions are hidden in data that AI processes. Like SQL injection, but for AI prompts. Important to understand if you're building AI-powered tools.

A technique that gives AI access to external data (documents, databases) at query time. Instead of relying only on training data, the model retrieves relevant information first, then generates an answer grounded in facts.
A cap on how many API requests you can make in a given time period. Prevents abuse and ensures fair access. If you hit one, you need to slow down or upgrade your plan.
A training technique where humans rate AI outputs, and the model learns to produce responses humans prefer. It's why modern AI feels more helpful and less robotic than earlier models.
A collection of tools, libraries, and documentation that makes it easier to build with an API. The Anthropic SDK lets you use Claude in your Python or JavaScript code with a few lines.
A secondary AI agent spawned by a primary agent to handle a specific subtask. Like delegating work to a team member. Multiple subagents can run in parallel on different parts of a project.
Hidden instructions given to an AI that set its behavior, personality, and rules before the user starts chatting. It's the difference between "generic AI" and "your custom agent."

A setting that controls how random or creative AI output is. Low temperature (0.0-0.3) = deterministic and focused. High temperature (0.7-1.0) = more creative and varied. Use low for code, high for brainstorming.
The basic unit AI uses to process text. A token is roughly 3/4 of a word. "Hamburger" is 3 tokens. Tokens determine cost (you pay per token) and fit within the context window.
The ability of AI to call external functions — search the web, read files, run code, access APIs. This is what separates agents from chatbots. Without tools, AI can only talk. With tools, it can act.
The neural network architecture behind all modern LLMs. Introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need." Uses attention mechanisms to process text in parallel rather than word by word.
A database designed to store and search embeddings (number representations of text/images). Used in RAG systems to find relevant documents quickly. Examples: Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma.
Synonym for parameters. The numerical values inside a neural network that determine how it processes input. Training adjusts the weights; inference uses them.

Asking AI to do something without giving it any examples. "Translate this to French" is zero-shot. Contrast with few-shot (providing examples first). Modern LLMs are surprisingly good at zero-shot tasks.
A prompting technique where you provide 2-5 examples of the desired input/output format before asking AI to process new input. Dramatically improves consistency and accuracy for structured tasks.

The practice of carefully curating what information you feed to AI — not just how you ask, but what data you include. More strategic than prompt engineering. The skill that separates casual users from power users.

A process where AI operates with autonomy: planning steps, using tools, evaluating results, and iterating without human intervention at each step. The opposite of chat-mode, where every exchange requires human input.

A multi-step workflow an agent knows how to execute by chaining tools together. "Deploy a website" is a skill (read files → build → deploy → verify). "Read file" is a tool. Tools are individual actions; skills are choreography. A good agent has: personality, goals, tools, and skills.

A RAG system built on your own knowledge base — blog posts, talks, documents, investor memos — so an AI can answer questions grounded in your actual expertise. Instead of generic AI answers, you get responses backed by your work. The new resume.

Splitting documents into smaller pieces for storage in a vector database. Chunk size is a critical design choice: too big and you retrieve irrelevant context, too small and you lose meaning. Typical sizes: 200-1,000 tokens per chunk.

Anchoring AI responses in real data (retrieved documents, search results, database records) rather than relying on training data alone. RAG is the most common grounding technique. Grounded answers cite sources; ungrounded answers hallucinate.

A pattern where sensitive AI actions (send email, delete files, deploy code) require human approval before execution. The agent proposes, the human approves. Critical for building trust and preventing costly mistakes.

A lightweight program that exposes tools to AI via the Model Context Protocol. One MCP server for Gmail means every AI app can send/read email. Build the server once; any MCP-compatible agent can use it.

An AI agent that coordinates other agents, breaking complex tasks into subtasks and assigning them. Like a project manager for AI teams. In multi-agent systems, the orchestrator decides who does what.

The process of splitting text into tokens — the fundamental units an LLM processes. Different models use different tokenizers, so the same text can produce different token counts. "Strawberry" might be 1 token or 3, depending on the tokenizer.

Quantization is like shrinking a high‑resolution photo into a smaller file by reducing the number of colors, but for neural nets. It drops the precision of the numbers the model uses (e.g., from 32‑bit floats to 8‑bit integers) so the model runs faster and needs less memory. The trade‑off is a tiny dip in accuracy, but for many apps the speed gain is worth it.

Model drift happens when a model's performance slides downhill because the real‑world data it encounters gradually differs from the data it was trained on. It's like a GPS that was calibrated for downtown streets but is now being used in a new suburb—the directions get less accurate over time. Detecting drift means regularly checking the model against fresh data and retraining when the error climbs beyond an acceptable threshold.

Think of a massive language model as a fully built Lego castle. An adapter is a small plug‑in block you snap onto the existing walls to give the castle a new ability without rebuilding it from scratch. You only train the adapter’s tiny set of weights, leaving the original model untouched, so you can quickly specialize for a new task or domain with far less compute.

Instruction tuning is like giving a student a cheat sheet of how to answer different types of questions before the exam. You train a language model on many examples where each prompt includes a clear instruction (e.g., 'Summarize the paragraph in one sentence') and the desired response. This helps the model follow new, unseen instructions more reliably, without needing full fine‑tuning on every task.

A model registry is like a library catalog for your AI models. It records each model version, its training data, performance metrics, and who approved it, so you can quickly find the right model for a job. When you pull a model from the registry, you know exactly which ‘book’ you’re reading, avoiding accidental mix‑ups or using stale models.

Asking the model to show its work step by step, like solving a math problem on paper instead of guessing the final answer. It improves accuracy by breaking complex tasks into smaller reasoning steps. Think of it as narrating your thinking out loud to get to a better conclusion.

Using knowledge gained while solving one problem and applying it to a different but related problem. It's like a carpenter who's great at building houses using those skills to build sheds more efficiently. Instead of training a model from scratch, you leverage pre-existing knowledge.

Knowledge distillation is like having a experienced teacher simplify complex lessons for a new student. It's a technique where a smaller, simpler model learns from a larger, more complex one, retaining the essential knowledge but making it more efficient. This helps deploy AI models in environments with limited resources, such as mobile devices or embedded systems. By distilling the knowledge, the smaller model can still make accurate predictions without needing the full complexity of the original model.

Dataset shift is like moving a restaurant to a new location - the menu stays the same, but the customers and their preferences change. In AI, it refers to the change in data distribution between training and testing, which can affect the model's performance. For example, a model trained on images of cars taken during the day may not perform well on images taken at night. This shift can happen due to changes in the environment, population, or other factors, and it's essential to consider it when training and deploying AI models.

Data augmentation is like photocopying a picture, then cutting it up and reassembling it to create new versions. This helps train AI models to be more robust by exposing them to different variations of the same data. For example, if you're training a model to recognize dogs, data augmentation might involve rotating, flipping, or adding noise to pictures of dogs to create new training examples.

Like making sure a new app works with your phone’s operating system — not every AI model can run on every platform or tool. Check compatibility before deploying, or it won’t start, scale, or respond the way you expect.

Gradient descent is like hiking down a mountain in thick fog. You can't see the bottom (the lowest error), so you feel around to find the steepest downward slope at your feet and take a step in that direction. Repeat until you're as low as you can get, hoping you've found the true bottom and not just a local dip.

Overfitting is like a student who memorizes the answers to a practice test instead of learning the material. They might ace the practice test, but they'll bomb the real thing because they don't understand the underlying concepts. In AI, overfitting happens when a model is too closely fit to the training data and doesn't generalize well to new, unseen data.

Regularization is like adding a stabilizer to a bike - it helps the model not to overfit the training data by reducing its complexity. Think of it as a way to prevent the model from becoming too specialized in the training examples, so it can generalize better to new, unseen data. This is achieved by adding a penalty term to the loss function, which discourages large weights.

The process of finding the optimal settings for your model that aren't learned from the data itself. These are knobs like learning rate or batch size that you set *before* training begins. Think of it as finding the perfect oven temperature and cooking time for a new recipe to get the best result.

This is when you train a model using data that has already been labeled with the correct answers. Think of it like teaching a child to identify fruits by showing them pictures of apples labeled 'apple' and bananas labeled 'banana'. The model learns to map inputs (like images) to outputs (like names) by minimizing errors between its predictions and your provided labels.

Exotic sampling is like searching for a specific type of rare seashell on a beach. Instead of randomly walking along the shore, you focus on areas where that shell is most likely to be found, increasing your chances of discovering it. In AI, this means using specialized techniques to sample data from regions of the input space that are most relevant to the task at hand, rather than sampling randomly. This approach can improve the efficiency and accuracy of model training and inference.

Data leakage is like having a cheat sheet for a test - it's when your model gets access to information it shouldn't have, which can make it seem smarter than it really is. This can happen when your training data includes information that won't be available when the model is actually used. For example, if you're training a model to predict stock prices based on news headlines, but the headlines include the stock prices themselves, that's data leakage. It can make your model look great during training, but perform poorly in the real world.

MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) is a set of practices for reliably and efficiently deploying and maintaining machine learning models in production. Think of it as DevOps for AI, covering everything from model development to continuous integration and delivery, monitoring, and retraining. It ensures your AI systems run smoothly and deliver value in the real world.

Latent space is a compressed, abstract representation of data where similar inputs are mapped closer together. Imagine it as a hidden map where every unique item in your dataset gets a specific, mathematically defined location based on its characteristics. This space allows models to understand underlying relationships and generate new, similar data points. It's where the 'meaning' of data is encoded.

Think of out-of-distribution like a GPS navigation system that's only been trained on city roads, but then you take it off-roading. It's when a model encounters data that's significantly different from what it was trained on, making it harder for the model to make accurate predictions. This can happen when there's a change in the environment, new types of data, or unexpected user behavior, and it's a key challenge in building robust AI systems.

An evaluation metric is like a report card for your AI model. It measures how well the model is doing its job, such as accuracy, precision, or recall. Think of it as a scorecard that helps you determine if your model is making good predictions or not. For example, in a spam detection model, the evaluation metric might be the percentage of correctly classified spam emails.

Data preprocessing is like preparing ingredients for a recipe. You need to clean, chop, and mix the data in the right way so your AI model can use it effectively. This step is crucial because bad data can lead to bad predictions, just like bad ingredients can ruin a dish. By preprocessing your data, you're setting your model up for success.

A centralized repository for managing and serving features for machine learning models. Think of it as a meticulously organized pantry for all the ingredients your models need, ensuring consistency across training and inference environments. It streamlines data access and helps prevent data duplication, making sure features are fresh and reliable.

The initial, extensive training of a large model on a massive, diverse dataset. This phase teaches the model broad knowledge and general patterns, much like a child learning general knowledge before specializing in a particular subject in school. The resulting pre-trained model can then be adapted for specific tasks via fine-tuning.

A knowledge graph is like a massive, interconnected spider web of information. It's a way to store and organize data as entities and their relationships, making it easy to query and reason about the information. For example, a knowledge graph for a movie database might have entities like 'movies', 'actors', and 'directors', and relationships like 'starring' or 'directed'. This allows you to ask complex questions like 'What movies has this actor been in?' and get accurate answers.

Knowledge retention is like a librarian keeping track of the books that are already on the shelves. It's the ability of a model to remember what it has learned from its training data, even when it's faced with new or unexpected information. This is important because it helps the model to avoid 'forgetting' what it already knows, and to build on its existing knowledge when learning new things.

Explainability is like trying to understand how a referee made a call in a sports game. You want to know the reasoning behind the decision, not just the outcome. In AI, explainability refers to the ability to interpret and understand the decisions made by a model, which is crucial for building trust and identifying potential biases. Think of it as getting a peek into the model's thought process.

A Foundation Model is a very large AI model, typically pre-trained on massive amounts of diverse, unlabeled data. It develops broad capabilities that can be adapted to many downstream tasks, often through fine-tuning. Think of it like a powerful, general-purpose operating system that can run many different applications once specialized, rather than a single-purpose app.

A Mixture of Experts (MoE) model uses several smaller, specialized neural networks (experts) and a 'router' to decide which expert processes each incoming piece of data. Think of it as a specialized consulting firm where the front desk directs your specific problem to the best-suited consultant. This allows the model to scale to many more parameters efficiently, as only a few experts are active for any given input.

Think of a knowledge graph as a massive, intricate web of relationships between entities. Knowledge Graph Embedding is like assigning a unique GPS coordinate to each entity in this web, so a model can understand how they relate to each other. This helps AI systems reason about complex relationships and make more informed decisions. For example, if 'Paris' and 'France' are close together in this embedded space, a model can infer that Paris is a city in France.

Data parallelism is like having multiple cooks in the same kitchen, each preparing the same dish but with different ingredients. This technique allows you to split your data into smaller chunks and process them simultaneously across multiple computing units, such as GPUs or CPUs, to speed up training times. By doing so, you can significantly reduce the time it takes to train large models on massive datasets. This approach is particularly useful when working with big data and complex models that require significant computational resources.

Think of data quality like the freshness of ingredients in a recipe. Just as a great chef can't make a delicious dish with rotten ingredients, a powerful AI model can't produce good results with low-quality data. Data quality issues, such as inconsistencies, missing values, or biases, can significantly impact the performance and reliability of AI systems.
